EPA/OPPT Multiple Process Vessel Residual Model, CEB standard 2% residual. User-Defined Loss Rate Model. Per ESD on the Blending of Fragrance Oils into Commercial and Consumer Products, "if the end-use product is unknown, a conservative estimate assumes that fragrance oil is used in powder products because conveying, mixing, and packaging powder products produce all forms of emissions, including dust emissions"; EPA suggests using a product loss fraction of 4.5% to estimate particulate emissions. Dust is typically passed through a cyclone to remove most particulate, followed by a scrubber or ESP to remove smaller particulate and vapors; EPA suggests assuming an air pollution control device efficiency of 85% (see ESD for additional details). Dust generation from conveying, mixing, and packaging powder can be estimated with a loss fraction of ~0.675% (LF = 0.045 * (1 - 0.85) =0.00675). Note that per the ESD, dust captured by control technologies is typically recycled back into the process and is not released into the environment. Therefore, this quantity is not estimated.
NAICS: water, air, incineration, or landfill (per ESD)

Basis: EPA/OPPT Drum Residual Model, CEB standard 3% residual. The ESD indicates that oil well chemicals may be transported in drums or bulk containers. If site-specific information is not available, EPA suggests that a 55-galllon drum be used as a default transport container to provide the most conservative release assessment. In lieu of additional industry-specific information, EPA conservatively assumes that empty containers may be rinsed with water or solvent, sent directly to a landfill or a drum recycler/re-conditioner. Therefore, container residues may be released to water (likely POTW), incineration or landfill.

User-Defined Loss Rate Model. Per the ESD, oil production equipment is unlikely to be cleaned frequently. Therefore, the ESD only quantifies releases of the chemical of interest from the disposal of "tank bottom residues". While some chemical may not be released to the environment via regular equipment cleaning, it is ultimately disposed to other media as this ESD is similar to a 100 percent release scenario. The ESD estimates approximately 0.0437% of the chemical by weight may be lost from the cleaning of storage tanks and separation vessels. Chemical contained in tank bottom residues may be disposed to water (e.g. surface discharge) or land (e.g. land-filling, land-spreading).

User-Defined Loss Rate Model. The ESD indicates that after water and sand are removed by gravity, the extracted oil/water mixture is separated through oil-water emulsion breaking. The oil well chemical may partition into either phase depending on its chemical and physical properties and presents several methods for estimating the partition (see ESD). If chemical-specific data are not available to estimate the partition, EPA recommends assuming 50 percent of the chemical partitions into the oil phase, with the remaining 50 percent remaining in the water phase, resulting in the following loss fraction (LF) = (1-Container Cleaning) x (1-Equipment Cleaning) x Fraction of PMN remaining in oil = (1-0.03) x (1-0.000437) x 0.5 = 0.485.

User-Defined Loss Rate Model. The ESD indicates that after water and sand are removed by gravity, the extracted oil/water mixture is separated through oil-water emulsion breaking. The oil well chemical may partition into either phase depending on its chemical and physical properties and presents several methods for estimating the partition (see ESD). If chemical-specific data are not available to estimate the partition, EPA recommends assuming 50 percent of the chemical partitions into the oil phase, with the remaining 50 percent remaining in the water phase, resulting in the following loss fraction (LF) = (1-Container Cleaning) x (1-Equipment Cleaning) x Fraction of PMN remaining in water phase = (1-0.03) x (1-0.000437) x 0.5 = 0.485. Of this water phase, 36% is deep-well injected and 1% is treated and discharged.
NAICS: deep well injection (36%) and wastewater treatment (1%) (per ESD)

Basis: User-Defined Loss Rate Model. Per the ESD, for on-shore operations, a small portion of the produced water is used for irrigation, transported to certified evaporation or percolation ponds, all of which ultimately result in land releases. The ESD presents the following loss fraction (LF) = (1-Container Cleaning) x (1-Equipment Cleaning) x Fraction of PMN remaining in water phase x Fraction of produced water released to land = (1-0.03) x (1-0.000437) x 0.5 x 0.06 = 0.029.

User-Defined Loss Rate Model. Per the ESD on Chemicals Used in Water Based Washing Operations at Industrial and Institutional Laundries, assume the entire production volume of the chemical of interest is discharged directly to a POTW from the washing process. Loss fraction = (1 - Fraction lost from container residue) = (1 - 0.03) = 0.97.

User-Defined Loss Rate Model. Per the ESD on Chemicals Used in Water Based Washing Operations at Industrial and Institutional Laundries, assume the entire production volume, except dust emissions, is discharged directly to a POTW from the washing process. LF = 1 - 0.005 - 0.995.

EPA/OPPT Solids Transfer Dust Loss Model. No dust controls are assumed as a worst case. Per the ESD on Chemicals Used in Water Based Washing Operations at Industrial and Institutional Laundries, "dust generation is expected from transferring operations"; EPA suggests using the EPA/OPPT Dust Emissions from Transferring Soilds Model to estimate dust releases generated during the transfer of solid laundry cleaning products. If additional site specific information is not  available, this release is conservatively assumed released to air, water, incineration, or land (per ESD).
NAICS: Air, Water, Incineration, or Landfill (per ESD)

Basis: EPA/OPPT Penetration Model. Per the ESD on Chemicals Used in Water Based Washing Operations at Industrial and Institutional Laundries, "for volatile chemicals, releases to air may occur as a worker manually pours the laundry cleaning product into the washer (default scenario)"; automatic liquid injection systems are only expected to generate air releases when transfer lines are being connected to the transport containers. EPA suggests using the EPA/OPPT Penetration Model to estimate releases from either manual or automatic loading. Manual loading is expected to occur over the course of 12 hours per day.

EPA/OPPT Penetration Model. Per the ESD on Chemicals Used in Water Based Washing Operations at Industrial and Institutional Laundries, "volatile chemicals may evaporate and be released to air during the washing and drying process." While most of these volatile releases will be vented outside the facility from the washer or dryer, a portion of volatile chemicals may be released into the workers breathing zone. EPA suggests using the EPA/OPPT Penetration Model to estimate volatile releases from a pool of liquid; "lifters" are typically located at industrial laundry facilities and are open vessels that process hot water from one stage of the washer to the next. The chemical of interest within the hot wash water will be at a dilute concentration; EPA recommends assuming 0.001 kg chemical of interest/kg of wash water. A vapor pressure correction factor can be estimated based on the use chemical properties (see ESD for additional information). // Note: Vapor correction factor shown based on a chemical of interest molecular weight of 200 g/mol.

User-Defined Loss Rate Model. Per the ESD on Chemicals Used in Water Based Washing Operations at Industrial and Institutional Laundries, "volatile components may be released to a POTW in wastewater after the washing cycle." They may also evaporate and be released to air during the washing process, especially if hot water washing cycle is used. Any residual volatile components that are not removed during the washing process will evaporate during the transfer, streaming, pressing, or drying of the laundered textile. Per ESD, assume the entire production volume of the chemical of interest, except for releases to air during transfers, is released to POTW or vented to air. Loss fraction = (1 - Fraction lost from container residue - Fraction lost from dust generation) = (1 - 0.03 - 0) = 0.97. (Note that this assumes that upstream fugitive air releases are negligible).

User-Defined Loss Rate Model. Per the ESD on Chemical Vapor Deposition in the Semiconductor Industry, unreacted CVD precursors from the deposition process are vented to control technology for treatment prior to release to the environment; the quantity of unreacted material purged is related to the utilization rate of the precursor. In the absence of chemical specific data, EPA recommends assuming 30% to 50% utilization rate for a given CVD precursor; the utilization rate corresponds to a high-end release fraction of 70% and a low end release fraction of 50%. EPA also assumes a default abatement removal and destruction of 99 percent. The remaining one percent is further routed to a central house abatement system, where potential releases include air or water.

EPA/OPPT Bulk Transport Residual Model, CEB standard 0.2% residual. Per the ESD on the Formulation and Application of Thermal and Carbonless Copy Paper Coatings, "information from industry sources indicates that almost all liquid raw materials are received at manufacturing facilities in bulk (tanker or railcar)"; EPA recommends assuming a default container size of 5,000 gallon tank trucks. Therefore, EPA suggests using the EPA/OPPT Bulk Transport Residual Model to estimate container residue releases from raw materials. If it is known that coating occurs on a relatively small scale, such as at a converter facility, the EPA/OPPT Drum Residual Model may be used to estimate container residual for drums containing between 20 and 100 gallons of liquid. Per ESD, no information on container cleaning procedures was available; therefore, potential releases to water, incineration or landfill may be assumed.

EPA/OPPT Multiple Process Vessel Residual Model, CEB standard 2% residual. EPA assumes these residues are typically sent to on-site wastewater treatment at CCP and thermal paper manufacturing sites. Converter sites may not necessarily have on-site wastewater treatment, and may instead discharge without treatment directly to a POTW.

The oversprayed coating, in the form of a mist, either settles to the floor and walls of the spray booth or other workspace where spraying occurs or is captured by the ventilation system; most spray booths and prep stations use a dry filter to capture coating mist and dust from the exhaust prior to the final emission. The oversprayed coating particles that are captured by the controls are disposed to either incineration or landfill (per ESD). EPA recommends assuming that shops use a dry filter with an average capture efficiency of 96%; the remaining 4% is released to air.
